title: SHE DISAPPEARED FOR FIVE MONTHS—THEN ELIZABETH REVEALED WHAT GOD HAD DONE
paragraphs: SHE DISAPPEARED FOR FIVE MONTHS—THEN ELIZABETH REVEALED WHAT GOD HAD DONE
She had lived with the ache for years. Then, when the impossible finally happened, Elizabeth did something unexpected: she disappeared from public view.
There are miracles you announce immediately.
And then there are miracles so tender, so unbelievable, so deeply connected to wounds you have carried for years that you almost need silence before you can speak.
Elizabeth knew something about that kind of silence.

Luke introduces her and her husband Zechariah with words that should stop anyone who has ever assumed suffering must mean somebody has failed God. They were righteous before God, walking faithfully in His commandments—and yet they were childless.
Faithful.
And hurting.
Obedient.
And waiting.
Loved by God.
And living with an unanswered prayer.
Those truths existed in the same house.
That matters.
Because somewhere, someone reading this has quietly wondered whether the closed door means God is angry.
You prayed.
Nothing changed.
You remained faithful.
Nothing changed.
You watched other people receive what you had begged God for.
Nothing changed.
Eventually, people stopped asking about your prayer because even they became uncomfortable with how long the answer was taking.
Maybe you stopped talking about it too.
Elizabeth would understand the world of long waiting.
Luke says that she and Zechariah “had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years” (Luke 1:7, KJV).
There is no need to sanitize that sentence.
They were old.
The years in which pregnancy would ordinarily have been expected had passed.
The dream appeared humanly finished.
And this is where the story becomes dangerous to despair.
Because God had not forgotten the address.
While Zechariah was serving as a priest before God, the angel Gabriel appeared and told him something that must have sounded almost unbearable in its beauty:
“Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard.”
Your prayer.
Is heard.
Imagine hearing those words after you had grown old carrying the evidence that seemed to say otherwise.
God's silence had never been proof of God's absence.

Gabriel announced that Elizabeth would bear a son. His name would be John. He would be great in the sight of the Lord and would go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah, preparing a people for the coming Lord.
This was not merely an elderly couple finally receiving a child.
Redemptive history was moving.
The forerunner of the Messiah was coming.
And after Zechariah returned home, Luke records the moment with breathtaking simplicity:
“And after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived, and hid herself five months, saying, Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men.”
Luke 1:24–25, KJV
Read it again slowly.
She conceived.
And then she hid herself.
The Greek of Luke 1:24 reads in part:
“καὶ περιέκρυβεν ἑαυτὴν μῆνας πέντε”
kai periekryben heautēn mēnas pente.
In straightforward English:
“and she kept herself hidden for five months.”
The verb περιέκρυβεν, from περικρύπτω, carries the sense of concealing or keeping hidden. Luke really does tell us that Elizabeth withdrew for five months.
But here we need humility.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us why.
Perhaps you have heard sermons saying she hid because she was ashamed.
Scripture does not say that.
Perhaps she feared what neighbors would think.
Scripture does not say that either.
Perhaps she wanted solitude with God.
Possible—but again, Scripture does not tell us.
We should never make the Bible say more than the Holy Spirit chose to reveal.
What Luke does reveal is far more beautiful.
He tells us what Elizabeth said while she was hidden.
“Thus hath the Lord dealt with me…”
Her attention was not ultimately on herself.
It was on the Lord.
This woman had spent years carrying a condition that, in her social world, brought what she herself called “reproach among men.”
Then God looked upon her.
That language is powerful.
Not because God had previously been ignorant of Elizabeth.
He had seen every year.
Every prayer.
Every disappointment.
Every family gathering.
Every private ache.
Every time she may have wondered whether motherhood would ever be hers.
When Elizabeth says God “looked on me,” she is describing His gracious intervention.
The God who had always seen her had now acted.
And maybe that is where this ancient woman steps out of the pages of Luke and sits beside some of us.
Because there are things you have carried so long that they have started becoming part of your identity.
The divorce.
The infertility.
The rejection.
The addiction you keep fighting.
The child who walked away.
The ministry that collapsed.
The betrayal nobody knows about.
The years you lost.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The sin you confessed but whose consequences still follow you.
The shame you cannot seem to silence.
People may know your name, but somewhere inside you there is another name you have been answering to.
Failure.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Dirty.
Forgotten.
Too late.
Elizabeth's culture had its word too.
Reproach.
But heaven was writing another sentence.
And before we turn Elizabeth's story into a promise that every earthly disappointment will eventually be reversed exactly as hers was, we need to stop.
That is not the Gospel.
Some faithful Christians will pray for children and never conceive.
Some will pray for marriages that still end.
Some will pray for healing and eventually meet Christ through death rather than physical recovery.
Some doors remain closed.
Some losses remain losses on this side of resurrection.
Elizabeth's story does not teach us that God owes every believer the earthly outcome they desperately desire.
It teaches us something deeper.
God sees.
God remembers His purposes.
God remains faithful.
And ultimately, God's answer to human shame is not that everybody receives the life they imagined.
God's answer is Jesus Christ.
That is where Elizabeth's story is going.
Her miracle was never merely about Elizabeth.
Her son would become a voice crying in the wilderness:
Prepare the way of the Lord.
John's entire life pointed beyond John.
Beyond Elizabeth.
Beyond Zechariah.
Toward Jesus.
And suddenly the five months of hiddenness become part of a much larger story.
While Elizabeth was hidden, God was preparing a witness.
While Zechariah was silent, God was preparing a voice.
While Israel waited, God was preparing the way.
And while humanity remained trapped beneath sin, God was moving history toward Bethlehem.
Do you see it?
The deepest scandal in Scripture is not an elderly woman becoming pregnant.
It is that the holy God would come near to guilty people.
The Son of God would take flesh.
Jesus Christ would walk among sinners.
He would touch the unclean.
Eat with the despised.
Welcome the rejected.
Call sinners to repentance.
Expose hypocrisy.
Forgive the guilty.
Carry our sin to the cross.
And rise from the grave.
Elizabeth said God had taken away her reproach among people.
At Calvary, something infinitely greater happened.
Christ bore the judgment our sin deserved so that everyone who repents and trusts in Him can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost to Himself.
Jesus does not merely improve your reputation.
He gives the repentant sinner a new standing before God.
He does not merely cover the scandal.
He redeems the sinner.
This is why the Gospel reaches places motivational speeches cannot touch.
Motivation can tell you to forgive yourself.
Jesus can actually forgive you.
Culture can tell you to reinvent yourself.
Jesus says you must be born again.
People can tell you your past does not matter.
Jesus does something better: He acknowledges the reality of sin, pays its debt at the cross, calls you to repentance, and begins transforming your life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are reading this while hiding too.
Not physically.
Nobody suspects anything.
Your profile looks fine.
You smile in photographs.
You know the worship songs.
You know Christian language.
But there is a room inside your soul you keep locked.
A secret habit.
A resentment.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
An affair nobody discovered.
Pride disguised as spirituality.
A prayer life that disappeared months ago.
A private compromise.
A wound you refuse to surrender.
A faith that looks alive publicly but is suffocating privately.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to make hidden people look respectable.
He came to bring us into the light.

There is a difference between Elizabeth's seclusion and sinful hiding. Scripture never accuses Elizabeth of wrongdoing for withdrawing. But Scripture repeatedly confronts the human instinct to hide sin from God.
Adam hid.
David concealed.
Peter denied.
Yet grace kept pursuing broken people.
Not grace that says, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace that says, “Come into the light.”
Repent.
Return.
Be forgiven.
Follow Christ.
You may have spent five months hiding.
Five years.
Twenty years.
But the number of years does not exhaust the mercy of Christ.
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not turn this moment into another emotional experience you forget tomorrow.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Ask for help where help is needed.
And if these words describe the battle in your soul, comment, “no more hiding.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that you need grace is one small way of refusing to keep pretending.
If you are exhausted but still fighting for your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, comment, “pray for me.”
Someone scrolling beneath this article may need to discover that they are not the only person who has cried behind a closed door.
Elizabeth eventually came out of seclusion.
And when Mary, newly carrying Jesus, entered Zechariah's house and greeted her, the child in Elizabeth's womb leaped.
Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
The hidden woman became a woman proclaiming blessing.
The woman associated with reproach was now standing inside the unfolding story of redemption.
And the child inside her was responding to the presence of the unborn Messiah.
Everything points toward Christ.
It always does.
Maybe your greatest testimony will not be that God gave you everything you requested.
Maybe it will be that when life did not become what you expected, Jesus became more precious than everything you thought you needed.
Maybe your story will be:
I was ashamed, but Christ called me into the light.
I was guilty, but Christ forgave me.
I wandered, but Christ brought me home.
I thought my story was over, but grace found me in a chapter I never wanted.
That is why stories like Elizabeth's should not stay trapped on somebody's screen.
Not as superstition.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God.
It does not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him, not through an algorithm.
But if this truth helped you, sharing it can be a simple act of witness. Let the Gospel travel farther than your screen.
Send this privately to someone carrying shame.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who is willing to listen.

If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered work, don't confuse the method with the Master. Christ alone deserves the glory. But your sharing, generosity, encouragement, and support can become practical tools through which biblical truth reaches another person.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because there are moments when testimony turns a comment section into a room full of people discovering they were never struggling alone.
Tell us:
What have you been waiting on God for?
Because somewhere between Elizabeth's unanswered years and the moment she whispered, “The Lord has dealt with me,” stands a truth every wounded believer eventually has to face:
God's faithfulness cannot always be measured by how quickly the story changes.
Elizabeth's womb was no longer empty.
But an even greater miracle was approaching.
John would be born.
John would prepare the way.
Jesus would come.
And Jesus would do what no answered earthly prayer could ever accomplish.
He would save sinners.
So if you are still in the hidden months...
If the answer has not appeared...
If shame keeps whispering your old name...
If people have already decided what your story means...
Do not mistake the unfinished chapter for the final sentence.
The God who saw Elizabeth sees His people still.
And for everyone who comes to Jesus in repentance and faith, shame does not get to write the ending.
The scars may remain.
The consequences may be real.
The waiting may continue.
But the final word belongs to Christ.
And when Jesus holds the pen, even the chapter you wanted erased can become the place where grace is remembered.
